content:
How should a Muslim invite others to Islam? The question matters to every Muslim who speaks about the faith, and it matters to their hearers, who are entitled to know whether the invitation comes with pressure or with argument.

The Quran answers it directly. Its verses on daʿwah, the call, set rules for the manner of the invitation as well as its content.

This article aims to provide context to those rules, insha'Allah, in six principles drawn from the verses and their classical commentators. The first verse is the frame for all of them: "Invite (all) to the Way of thy Lord with wisdom and beautiful preaching; and argue with them in ways that are best and most gracious" (16:125).[1]

Al-Ṭabarī explains each term of the verse. Wisdom is the revelation God sends and His Book; beautiful preaching is the lessons God sets in His Book as proofs; and to argue "in ways that are best" is to overlook the harm done to one's own honour while never failing to deliver the message. Mujāhid, he records, glossed it: turn away from their harm.[2]

The verse ends with God's knowledge, "for thy Lord knoweth best, who have strayed from His Path, and who receive guidance".[1] The caller is responsible for the manner of the call, and God for its outcome.

"Let there be no compulsion in religion: Truth stands out clear from Error" (2:256). To the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself the Quran says: "wilt thou then compel mankind, against their will, to believe!" (10:99).[1]

Al-Fārūqī drew the conditions of daʿwah from these verses. The hearer must be free of fear and pressure, since the judgement sought is his own, and "a forced judgment is a contradiction in terms".[3] He put the rule more strongly elsewhere: "calling" is "certainly not coercing", and coerced daʿwah is "a grave violation of the human person, second only to homicide, if not equal to it".[4] We set out the verse and its history in no compulsion in religion.

"O People of the Book! come to common terms as between us and you: That we worship none but Allah; that we associate no partners with him; that we erect not, from among ourselves, Lords and patrons other than Allah" (3:64).[1]

The common ground the verse offers is real, and it is precise: the worship of God alone. The verse does not hide the disagreement. It names the point on which the disagreement turns, and it ends with the Muslims' own witness: "Bear witness that we (at least) are Muslims."[1]

"Dispute ye not with the People of the Book, except with means better (than mere disputation), unless it be with those of them who inflict wrong (and injury): but say, 'We believe in the revelation which has come down to us and in that which came down to you; Our Allah and your Allah is one'" (29:46).[1]

The verse regulates debate and does not forbid it, and it gives the words to begin with: a shared faith in God and in revelation. Issa Khan and his colleagues at the University of Malaya find in the Quran, the Sunnah and the caliph ʿUmar's treatment of other faiths a basis for dialogue built on justice, equal rights and freedom of belief.[5]

"Revile not ye those whom they call upon besides Allah, lest they out of spite revile Allah in their ignorance" (6:108).[1] The verse forbids insult even where the worship is false in the Quran's own judgement.

A Muslim may say plainly that the Trinity is a mistake, that an idol cannot hear, or that atheism fails. He may not mock what another holds sacred. The line is between an argument and an insult, and the Quran draws it.

"It is true thou wilt not be able to guide every one, whom thou lovest; but Allah guides those whom He will" (28:56). "Therefore do thou give admonition, for thou art one to admonish. Thou art not one to manage (men's) affairs" (88:21 to 22).[1]

If guidance is God's, the caller has no need to force a result. He can admit what he does not know, correct an error, and leave a conversation unfinished. Jaeho Chung, a Catholic missiologist in Rome, argues that both Christian mission and Islamic daʿwah, understood as witness through one's way of life and never as coercion, carry an intrinsic respect for the other.[6]

The bottom line

The Quran's rules for daʿwah are clear: invite with wisdom and good counsel, never compel, begin from real common ground, argue in the better way, insult no one's sacred things, and leave guidance to God. Al-Ṭabarī read 16:125 as patience under insult, and al-Fārūqī called coerced daʿwah a violation of the person second only to homicide.

Those rules make no concession on truth. The invitation is to the worship of God alone, and it is made with conviction. Its manner is fixed by the same revelation that gives its content: "Say, 'The truth is from your Lord': Let him who will believe, and let him who will, reject (it)" (18:29).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 16:125; 2:256; 10:99; 3:64; 29:46; 6:108; 28:56; 88:21 to 22; 18:29, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on Quran 16:125, Arabic text read on quran.com; the English is our paraphrase.
  3. Ismail R. al Faruqi and Lois Lamya al Faruqi, The Cultural Atlas of Islam (New York: Macmillan, 1986), p. 188.
  4. Ismail R. al Faruqi, Essential Writings, ed. Imtiyaz Yusuf (Leesburg, Va.: Center for Islam in the Contemporary World, and Petaling Jaya: Islamic Book Trust, 2021), "On the Nature of Islamic Da'wah", p. 124, from International Review of Mission 65, no. 260 (1976), p. 391.
  5. Issa Khan, Mohammad Elius, Mohd Roslan Mohd Nor and others, "A Critical Appraisal of Interreligious Dialogue in Islam", SAGE Open 10, no. 4 (2020), doi:10.1177/2158244020970560.
  6. Jaeho Chung, "Dialogue Between Christian Mission and Islamic Da'wah", Religions 17, no. 8 (2026), article 932, doi:10.3390/rel17080932.
